porbos.title: What We Mean by Jahiliyyah • Unless You Know the Darkness, You Cannot Know the Light • Three Hundred and Sixty Objects of Worship • One Sentence, and Everything Changed • We Have No Idols in Our Homes, Yet • How Helpless Women Were • The Day He Spoke of Women

blocks.1: Let us begin today’s lesson with one word. Jahiliyyah. The word comes from ‘jahl’. Jahl means not knowing, ignorance. But there is a risk of a misunderstanding here, so let me make the matter clear at the very outset. Jahiliyyah does not mean that they were fools. Not at all. They could memorise a poem of a thousand lines after hearing it once. They found their way across the desert by the positions of the stars. They could recite genealogies from memory down thirty generations. Their language was one of the richest in the world. For the camel alone their dictionary held hundreds of words. And it was not only intelligence. When a guest came, they would slaughter even their last camel to feed him. If there was no food in the house, they would go hungry themselves and feed the guest. When they gave their word, they kept it even at the cost of their lives. They counted lying as cowardice.
blocks.2: There is no need even to speak of courage. No empire ever made them bow their heads. And their bodies were like iron. The desert sun and days upon days of hunger could not overpower them. So in what way were they ignorant? Here lies the real point. Jahiliyyah does not mean a lack of information. Jahiliyyah means a lack of direction. There is intelligence in the head, but no knowing in which direction to use it. There is strength in the hand, but it has not been settled for whom that strength is to be spent. A lamp is burning. It has oil, it is giving light; but no one is holding it in hand to show the way. The lamp lies in a heap of straw. Then that very light becomes a fire. The condition of Arabia was exactly that. Everything good in it was being spent in the wrong direction.
blocks.3: So what we mean by Jahiliyyah is a condition in which a person does not know where he came from, why he came, and where he will go after death. And this is exactly why the Qur’an did not keep the word as merely the name of an era. The Qur’an speaks of ‘the assumption of Jahiliyyah’, ‘the judgement of Jahiliyyah’, ‘the adornment of Jahiliyyah’, ‘the zealotry of Jahiliyyah’. That is, Jahiliyyah is not the name of a date. It is the name of a condition. A condition that can return in any age, in any land.
blocks.4: So today’s lesson is not only history from fourteen hundred years ago. First we will see what that darkness was like. Then we will see what he changed when he came. And at the end we will return to today’s world; we will see how much of that darkness remains even now, only with its name changed.
blocks.5: Unless You Know the Darkness, You Cannot Know the Light
blocks.6: Let me begin today’s lesson with one remark. If you tell someone, this man is very good, he will not understand. But if you say, when the whole neighbourhood was setting fires, this man alone was running about with a bucket in his hand; then he will understand. Worth is understood in context. Today we will see the context of the Prophet {{1}}. Where he came, among whom he came, what the people of that land saw as they grew up; unless we know that, we will never understand what he brought.
blocks.7: So the first half of today’s lesson is hard. Hard, because here we will see blood. We will see a child buried in the earth. We will see a woman bound with rope. We will see people sold. Dear reader, do not look away. Without seeing this much darkness you will never understand the worth of that light. A house in Makkah. Morning. A father is dressing his little daughter. How old might the girl be? Five, or six. Oil has been put in her hair. It has been combed neatly. The best dress she has has been put on her. She sits quietly. She does not move at all, lest the adornment go wrong. Her father has never dressed her up like this before. Surely today is some special day.
blocks.8: The father took her hand. The two of them opened the door and went out. The houses ran out. The wells ran out. Even the last date palm was left behind. Then only sand. The girl’s feet are small. To keep pace with one step of her father she has to take two. Still she does not let go of his hand. Father, how much further! After going a very long way the father stopped. There was no one around. Nothing but the sound of the wind. He knelt down. Then he began to dig the ground. The girl stands beside him, watching. As he digs, dust rises. Dust settles on the father’s head, on his shoulders, in his beard.
blocks.9: The girl came a little closer. Then she stretched out her small hand and began to brush the dust from her father’s beard. The father digs. The daughter brushes off the dust. The pit was made. The father stood up. He lifted the girl in both hands. For one moment the girl thought that her father was taking her into his arms. Then the earth. One handful. Two handfuls. Three handfuls. A call was coming from below. The father did not stop. Then there was no sound any more.
blocks.10: Brushing the dust from his hands, he stood up. Then he took the road to the city. Alone. Many years later. The Mosque of Madinah. A man came and stood before the Prophet {{1}}. Then he told this very event in his own words. The Prophet {{2}} wept. As he wept, his blessed beard became wet.{{3}}
blocks.12: The girl’s bones are no more by then. There is no one to complain. There is no one to seek justice. No one even wrote down her name. Only one person wept. This was the society into which he came.
blocks.13: Three Hundred and Sixty Objects of Worship
blocks.14: A stone house in the middle of Makkah. Many, many years ago two men raised the foundations of this house with their own hands. Father and son; Ibrahim and Isma‘il (AS). One handing up the stones, the other setting them in place. And on the lips of both, one single prayer.
blocks.16: Our Lord! Accept this from us.{{1}}
blocks.17: Why was the house being built? So that there might be on the face of the earth one place where only One would be called upon. No stone would be there. No idol would be there. No middleman would be there. Only the servant, and his Lord. And think once of the life of the one who was building the house. He was the son of a people who worshipped idols. His own father made idols. One day, when everyone went out for a festival, the young Ibrahim entered the temple. An axe in his hand.{{1}}
blocks.18: He broke the idols one after another. Then, leaving the biggest, he hung the axe on its shoulder. The people returned and cried out, who has done this? He said, that big one did it. Then he added—
blocks.20: So ask these very ones, if they are able to speak.{{1}}
blocks.21: The people bowed their heads. A god that cannot remove even the axe from its own body, how will it remove people’s troubles? The foundation of the House of the Ka‘bah was laid by the hands of this very man. And before leaving, he made a supplication.
blocks.23: My Lord! … Keep me and my children far from the worship of idols.{{1}}
blocks.24: Now the door of that house. Two and a half thousand years later.{{1}}
blocks.25: Rows upon rows of idols. Some of stone. Some of wood. Some of gold. Counted, the number comes to three hundred and sixty. One idol for one tribe. Another for another tribe. Each with its own object of worship. And who are those bowing their heads before them? They are the descendants of Ibrahim (AS) himself. That supplication had been made for them. The hand that once broke idols with an axe, the descendants of that very hand brought idols and set them up. When the lamp itself becomes a container of darkness, what hope is left?
blocks.26: Here one thing must be understood very well. Otherwise the whole matter will be misunderstood. The Arabs were not atheists. They knew who had made the heavens and the earth.
blocks.28: And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, Allah.{{1}}
blocks.29: When a storm rose at sea, they called upon Allah. Their children were named ‘Abdullah; the name of the Prophet’s {{1}} father was exactly that. So where was the problem? The problem was in a single word. The middleman. They said, Allah is so great. We are such small people, how can we go straight to Him? The Qur’an has set out this argument of theirs exactly as it was.
blocks.31: They say, We worship them only so that they may bring us closer to Allah.{{1}}
blocks.32: They are not saying, there is no Allah. They are saying, Allah exists; but a ladder is needed to reach Him. And that very ladder became the object of worship. This is how shirk comes. No one says in a single day, leave Allah out. They only say, add another alongside Allah. One thing makes clear how far the matter went. They performed Hajj. They circled the Ka‘bah. They recited the talbiyah too. Labbayka la sharika laka labbayk. You have no partner; here I am at Your service. The statement is right indeed. But after that they would add a line: except for that partner who is Yours.{{1}}
blocks.33: With their mouths they say, You have no partner. And within that very sentence they seat a partner. In one hand tawhid. In the other shirk. And carrying both together they circle the House of Allah. Inside the Ka‘bah, before Hubal, a young man is standing. His hand is trembling. He wants to marry a girl. But the decision is not his. The attendant drew arrows from the quiver. On one was written ‘yes’. On another, ‘no’. The arrows were shaken. One came out. ‘No.’ The young man went out with his head bowed. Going on a journey? That arrow. Starting a business? That arrow. The fate of a whole nation hung on the spinning of a piece of wood.
blocks.34: But the greatest emptiness was not in the idols. It was in the Hereafter. That there will be an accounting after death; this was laughable to them. One day a man brought an old bone. He crushed it to powder inside his fist. Then, scattering it in the wind, he said, who will bring this to life? He did not know that the answer to this very saying of his would come down from heaven. What is the result of lacking this one belief? A person who knows that he will never have to answer cannot be held back by anything. If no one is watching, he is free. And the roots of all the rest of Jahiliyyah’s darkness are right here.
blocks.36: In place of the three hundred and sixty idols he set one sentence. La ilaha illa Allah. The sentence begins with ‘no’. First remove everything. Remove the stones, remove the arrows, remove the middleman. Empty the house. Then seat the One. People asked, what is your Lord like? What is His lineage? In reply a short surah came down.{{1}}
blocks.38: Say, He is Allah, One. Allah is the Self-Sufficient. He neither begot nor was begotten. And there is none comparable to Him.{{1}}
blocks.39: Four sentences. The answer to three hundred and sixty idols ended in four sentences. And the greatest work he did elsewhere. In Surah al-Fatihah Allah taught the servant a phrase.
blocks.41: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.{{1}}
blocks.42: You alone. No ladder. No intercessor. And He brought it even closer.
blocks.44: And when My servants ask you about Me, then I am indeed near; I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me.{{1}}
blocks.45: In other verses Allah says to the Prophet {{1}}, ‘Say’. And in this verse even that word is not there. He said directly, I am near. To a people who thought that a ladder was needed to reach Allah, it was said, He is nearer to you than your jugular vein.{{2}}
blocks.46: From the talbiyah too that added line was wiped away. Now only this remained: la sharika lak. No more ‘but’. No more ‘except’. Then that day came. The day of the conquest of Makkah. He entered the House. A staff in his hand. And as he broke the idols one by one, he was reciting—
blocks.48: And say, ‘The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood was ever bound to vanish.’ Surah Bani Isra’il, verse 81{{1}}
blocks.49: The darkness of centuries ended in a single day. The one who broke the idols that day with a staff in his hand, whose descendant was he? Ibrahim’s (AS). Who once broke idols with an axe in his hand. And who had prayed, keep me and my children far from the worship of idols. The prayer was accepted. It only took a few centuries’ delay.
blocks.50: Those arrows for seeing fate were forbidden.
blocks.52: O believers! Wine, gambling, altars for idols and divining arrows; these are but the work of Satan. So avoid them.{{1}}
blocks.53: And the answer to the man who had crushed the bone and scattered it in the wind also came down.
blocks.55: He says, who will bring these rotten bones to life? Say, the One who created them the first time will bring them to life.{{1}}
blocks.56: And this one belief alone changed people from within. Even the wrong that no one was watching now stopped. Because One is watching. In the time of ‘Umar (RA), a shepherd boy was told, sell one sheep; the owner will not know. The boy said, let the owner not know; Allah knows.{{1}}
blocks.57: We Have No Idols in Our Homes, Yet
blocks.58: No one’s home has an idol. But an amulet hangs on the wall of the house. Something hangs on the car mirror so the evil eye does not strike. Before an exam, some people turn the pages of the newspaper and check their horoscope. Printed letters instead of arrows. But no one notices that the hand is being stretched out in the same place. And the middleman too remains. When work is stuck, people run to the shrine. No child; a vow. Must win a case; a vow. There, hands are raised and it is said, you put in a word for me. The argument is the same. I am a sinner; why would Allah hear me? An argument from fourteen hundred years ago. Fourteen hundred years later, the same. Yet he had said, I am near.
blocks.59: Allah’s right, however, is not only the right to be worshipped. There is another right, about which we speak much less. The right to command. That is, which is right and which is wrong, which is lawful and which is unlawful; who will decide that?
blocks.61: The right to command belongs to Allah alone.{{1}}
blocks.62: The matter is actually very simple. The one who made the clock writes the rules for how the clock will run. And the One who made man has Himself written how man should run. Going back once more to Jahili Arabia, the picture is this. They did not deny Allah. But when taking decisions in life, whose word did they listen to? That arrow placed before Hubal. Allah exists; but life will run on the word of the arrow. They accepted Allah as Creator. They did not accept Him as Ruler.
blocks.63: Today there are no arrows in our homes. But on whose word is the decision made? When dividing the father’s property, which calculation do we open? When a business involves interest, yet the profit is good; whose argument wins then? When taking dowry at a daughter’s wedding, which rule do we follow? Allah’s rule? Or society’s rule? And the greatest test comes another way. The polytheists, to protect the honour of their idols, would change their own decisions. And today? Today when the leader says one thing, we push Allah’s word to the back. When the party’s decision collides with Allah’s command, we side with the party. Out of fear of what society will say, we drop the command. In those days positions changed out of respect for idols. Today, to please people. The name has changed. Has the place of the test changed?
blocks.64: Let there be no misunderstanding here. The leader may be respected. The party may be loved. Society may be heeded. The country may be loved. Islam has forbidden none of these. It has only set a limit. The Prophet {{1}} said, obedience is only in what is right.{{2}}
blocks.65: There is no obedience to any creature in disobedience to the Creator. I will follow the leader, so long as he does not command disobedience to Allah. I will respect society, but not by sacrificing Allah’s law. I will love my country, but not by forgetting Allah. Because the believer’s ultimate obedience is for One alone. Jahiliyyah does not always return in the same dress. Sometimes it comes in the name of idols. Sometimes in the name of personality worship. Sometimes in the name of blind party loyalty. Sometimes in the name of social pressure. Sometimes in the name of national sentiment. The name changes. The face changes. The method changes. But the work inside stays the same. Handing Allah’s right over to human hands. The sentence La ilaha illa Allah begins with ‘no’. First one must remove. Then one must seat. We have seated. We have not removed. So merely saying ‘I believe in Allah’ with the mouth is not enough. The real test comes on the day when Allah’s command stands directly opposite my interest.
blocks.66: On that day whom will I choose? The leader, or Allah? The party, or Allah? Society, or Allah? My own heart’s desire, or Allah? That shepherd boy said, let the owner not know; Allah knows. In this one sentence lies the whole lesson of tawhid.
blocks.68: A house in Makkah. The last part of the night. Inside, the pains of childbirth are going on. Out in the courtyard sits the father. Before dawn a sound of crying came. A new voice. The midwife opened the door and came out. She gave the news. A daughter. The father stood up. He said nothing. He went out. And inside the house the mother lies. Her body is giving way with the exhaustion of having just given birth. Beside her the small body. She looked at the face. And in that very moment her heart went cold. Because a girl had been born in this house once before. She is no longer in the house. Even so she took the girl to her breast. Days passed. Months passed. The girl began to grow. The first day she smiled, the mother smiled. The first day she stood up, the mother held out both hands and held her. And the first day she called ‘Mother’, she burst into tears.
blocks.69: The girl did not understand why her mother was crying. When putting her to sleep at night, she would look at her face for a long time. And every night the same thought came to mind. One day someone will come and ask for this hand. How does it feel? Knowing that the child you are putting to sleep in your arms will one day have her grave dug, still feeding her every day, combing her hair, stroking her head all night when fever comes! Then that day came. In the morning the father sat down to dress the girl. The mother watched from afar. She understood. Did she step forward? Did she sit down at her husband’s feet? Did she say, keep her; I’ll give her my own share of food? History did not write it down. Only this much is known: that morning two people went out of that house.
blocks.70: And she stood holding the door. In the evening one returned. The husband came into the house. He washed his hands. He ate. Then he fell asleep. And that night, in one corner of the house, a mother stayed awake. The girl’s clothes were still lying in the house. No one asked her, how are you feeling. Another house. Evening. The husband called his wife. The woman came. She stood before him. The husband said, go to such-and-such man of such-and-such tribe. Bring his child. The man is a hero. The man’s lineage is great. If we have such a child, the honour of our house will rise. The woman raised her face and looked. Then she said nothing. There was no place to speak. She drew aside the curtain and went out. After some months she came back. The husband was then happy. The honour of the house will rise; the lineage will grow great. In due time the child was born.
blocks.71: There was a celebration in the tribe. People came and congratulated the father. And the woman sat in a corner. Then she spent the rest of her life in that very house. She raised the child of her own womb, a child who was not her husband’s. What was going on inside her, no one ever asked. The custom even had a name. Nikah al-Istibda‘.{{1}}
blocks.72: It has a name, it has rules, it has society’s recognition. That is, this is no lone madness of some depraved man; this was the system. The custom was given a name. No one gave the woman a name. An alley in Madinah. On the doors of a few houses, cloth flags hung. Everyone in the city knows what the flags mean. Even small children know. Inside one such house sits a girl. Her name is Musaykah. She is the slave-girl of the owner of the house. The owner’s name is ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy; the hypocrite chief of Madinah. Evening is falling. In a little while she will have to open the door. She sits. The money gathered by the end of the night she must hand into the owner’s hand in the morning. Once she had said, I will not do it. That day she was beaten. In this house she has another companion. Her name is Umaymah. Her condition is the same.
blocks.73: Two girls. Both want to remain chaste. They want to. She wants to, but cannot. Because the very body with which she is made to sin is not even her own! In another house, talaq came. The husband divorced her. The woman went to her father’s house. The ‘iddah began. Just before the ‘iddah ended the husband came and said, I take her back. She returned. After some days again talaq. Again her father’s house. Again taking her back on the last day of the ‘iddah. Again. Again. Again. There was no limit. The man would neither keep her nor release her. He knew that if he released her, the woman would get free. She would make a home elsewhere, perhaps even be happy. So he did not release her. For years he kept her hanging. Neither at home. Nor free. What easier way is there to torment a person?
blocks.74: In another house news came that the husband had died in battle. A wail of weeping rose in the house. The first day of grief had not even ended. In the meantime someone stood at the door. The dead man’s son; a child of another wife’s house. He came in. Then he threw the cloth in his hand over the widow’s body. Everyone knew the meaning of this cloth too. The woman is now his.{{1}}
blocks.75: If he wished he would marry her. If he wished he would give her in marriage elsewhere and take the mahr himself. If he wished he would keep her confined all her life, until the woman bought her freedom with everything she had. A little while ago she had been the mistress of the house. Now she is a piece of goods belonging to that same house. From her husband’s property she received nothing. Because she herself was a part of that property.
blocks.76: The calculation was this. Born, she is a burden. After marriage, she is a means to raise the house’s honour. When the husband dies, she is inheritance property. A whole life from birth to death; and at not a single turn of that life did anyone ever once ask her, what do you want. No one in the world wept for these girls. No poet wrote a single line in their names.
blocks.77: The Day He Spoke of Women
blocks.78: Then one came. He had not brought any army. He had not brought any book of law. He came with a few sentences. And those very sentences opened the doors of those houses. The Mosque of Madinah. The Prophet {{1}} was sitting. Around him the Companions. He said, whoever raises two daughters, nurturing them until they grow up, on the Day of Resurrection he and I will be like this. As he said it, he joined two of his fingers together to show.{{2}}
blocks.79: The gathering fell silent. These people had come from that society where at the news of a daughter’s birth the father’s face went dark. Where the calculation was made, shall we keep her in the house, or bury her in the ground? And now they were being told, by holding that girl’s hand you will enter Paradise. The girl who was the burden of the house became a ladder to Paradise. And the girl whom no one came to save! Who was buried under the earth, whose name no one wrote down! For her Allah set a question on the plain of Resurrection.
blocks.81: And when the girl buried alive is asked, for what crime was she killed.{{1}}
blocks.82: The question is not being put to the killer. The question is put to her. She, whose word no one in the world ever heard even once, the whole plain of Gathering will stand that day and listen to her. Our mother ‘A’ishah (RA) has described four kinds of marriage in the Jahili age. One kind was real marriage. The other three were fornication; only the name was marriage. She ended the account with one sentence. ‘Then when Muhammad {{1}} came with the truth, he demolished all the marriages of the Jahili age; except one.’{{2}}
blocks.83: One sentence. And in that one sentence three darknesses went out. The husband who used to send his wife to another, that right of his ended. The woman whose child’s father was settled by the pointing of a finger, her child will now get a certain name. And the flags hung at the mouths of the alleys came down. Then he did one thing more. He said, the guardian must not give a virgin girl in marriage without taking her permission.{{1}}
blocks.84: The Companions asked, O Messenger of Allah! A virgin is shy; how will she give permission? He said, her silence is her permission. In a society where a girl was never asked anything, now even her silence is being heard. Do you remember that alley? Where flags hung on doors. Where Musaykah sat waiting for evening. One day she could bear it no more. Breaking through every barrier she came out. Passing the alley, passing the market, she walked towards the mosque. Then she went and stood before the Prophet {{1}}. And, weeping, she told everything. That very day the answer came from heaven.
blocks.86: And do not compel your slave-girls to fornication, if they wish to remain chaste, in order to seek the goods of worldly life.{{1}}
blocks.87: A person of the lowest rung of society. One whose own name was not meant to be in history. In answer to that girl’s weeping the Lord of the Throne Himself spoke. Not only that. The man who was doing this wrong was one of the most influential people of Madinah. The verse did not name anyone. But the whole of Madinah understood whom it was speaking of. From that day the owner’s right over the slave-girl’s body was lifted forever. And He made the freeing of slaves one of the greatest righteous deeds.
blocks.88: For the one who was kept hanging year after year, two verses came down. The first set the limit.
blocks.90: Divorce is twice; then either retention in a proper manner or release with kindness.{{1}}
blocks.91: The game of endless divorce ended. And the second verse caught directly the very intention that no one had been able to catch until then.
blocks.93: And do not keep them back to harm them, in order to transgress.{{1}}
blocks.94: The matter is subtle. The man did not lock the house. He did not beat her either. Looking from outside, nothing could be understood. He only did not release her. In human courts this crime did not even have a name. And Allah sent down a verse in the Qur’an for that unnamed crime. Do you remember that widow? The one over whom a cloth was thrown? For her this verse came down.
blocks.96: O believers! It is not lawful for you to inherit women by force.{{1}}
blocks.97: The custom of throwing the cloth ended that very day. But Allah did not stop here. The woman who herself was part of the property, He made the owner of property.
blocks.99: For men there is a share in what parents and close relatives leave behind, and for women too there is a share; whether it be little or much, a fixed share.{{1}}
blocks.100: The Arabs were stunned on hearing this verse.{{1}}
blocks.101: They said, she who does not ride a horse, who does not fight, who is of no use to the tribe’s work; why should she get a share of wealth? Allah gave no explanation. He only said, a fixed share. The twenty-three years of prophethood were almost over. The plain of ‘Arafah. The Farewell Hajj. Before him more than a hundred thousand people. Many of whose fathers had once buried their daughters in the ground with their own hands. He is seated on a camel. This sermon was his last great sermon. He knew there was no time after this. At such a moment people say the most important things. He said, fear Allah regarding women.{{1}}
blocks.102: The whole of Arabia stood that day and heard those words. In the very land where once a woman’s name came up alongside the camel, standing before hundreds of thousands of people he spoke of women. And that very saying is recited even today from every Friday pulpit. This change came about in twenty-three years. Not by any army. Not by setting up any court. By changing what is inside people. The hand that once dug a daughter’s grave learned to stroke a daughter’s head. And this is no story. This is history.

quiz.q: What is the simile of the burning lamp lying in a heap of straw used to convey?
o: Strength without direction brings only destruction
Direction is of no use without strength
With light, the path is found by itself
Lighting a lamp in darkness is hard work
quiz.e: The lamp is burning, there is oil too; but no one is holding it in hand to show the way. Then that very light becomes a fire.

quiz.q: Despite being extraordinary in memory, language and poetry, why were they called ‘jahil’?
o: They knew nothing of reading and writing
Their language itself was incomplete
Their memory was weak
That strength had no purpose
quiz.e: Jahiliyyah does not mean a lack of information; Jahiliyyah means a lack of direction.

quiz.q: Besides the supplication made when raising the foundations of the Ka‘bah, the other prayer that came in Surah Ibrahim is
o: To keep the children away from idol-worship
To grant the children vast wealth and land
To protect the children from enemies
To grant the children long life
quiz.e: Surah Ibrahim, verse 35; My Lord, keep me and my children far from the worship of idols.

quiz.q: After breaking the idols in the temple and hanging the axe on the big one’s shoulder, what did Ibrahim (AS) say to the people?
o: I do not know who came and did this
Ask these very ones, if they can speak
I myself have done this, forgive me
Your big one told me everything
quiz.e: Surah al-Anbiya’, verse 63; pointing to the big one he said, ask these very ones.

quiz.q: According to Surah Luqman, verse 25, what would the polytheists answer when asked who created the heavens and the earth?
o: Al-Lat and al-‘Uzza did
Hubal created them
Allah created them
This is not known to us
quiz.e: They were not atheists; asked about the Creator, they would surely say, Allah.

quiz.q: In Surah al-Zumar, verse 3, what argument did the polytheists give in support of their worship?
o: These were made by the hands of our forefathers
These themselves created the heavens and the earth
These arrange our sustenance
These bring us near to Allah
quiz.e: They said, we worship them only so that they may bring us near to Allah.

quiz.q: In the Jahili talbiyah, what is the meaning of the line they added after ‘la sharika laka’?
o: Except that partner who is Yours
Except that partner who is greater than You
Except that partner whom You sent
Except that partner who is our forefather
quiz.e: While denying a partner with the mouth, within that very sentence they set a partner.

quiz.q: Which decisions did they take by the arrows placed before Hubal in the Ka‘bah?
o: Decisions of war, peace and taxes
Decisions of marriage, travel and business
Decisions of Hajj, sacrifice and vows
Decisions of crops, water and pastures
quiz.e: On one ‘yes’, on one ‘no’; even whether a child was one’s own was settled by these arrows.

quiz.q: Placing Ibrahim’s (AS) prayer beside the three hundred and sixty idols of the Ka‘bah, which lesson is obtained?
o: Lineage is the means to hold on to the religion
Lineage cannot hold on to the religion
Prophets’ prayers are not delayed in acceptance
If a prayer is not accepted, the fault is the supplicant’s
quiz.e: The hand that once broke idols with an axe, the descendants of that very hand brought idols and set them up.

quiz.q: What was the real form of the Jahili Arabs’ shirk?
o: Not accepting Allah as Creator
Denying the existence of Allah
Taking a medium to reach Allah
Denying the heavenly Books
quiz.e: They said, Allah is very great; a ladder is needed to reach Him. And that very ladder became the object of worship.

quiz.q: What special aspect of Surah al-Baqarah, verse 186 is shown in the lesson?
o: The verse also mentions the Prophet’s ﷺ name
The verse is the shortest verse of the Qur’an
The word ‘say’ itself is not in the verse
The verse was not revealed in Madinah
quiz.e: In other verses Allah says ‘say’ to the Prophet ﷺ; here He speaks directly, I am near.

quiz.q: On the day of the conquest of Makkah, which verse was the Prophet ﷺ reciting as he broke the idols with a staff in his hand?
o: Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful
Today I have perfected for you this religion
When the help of Allah and the great victory come
The truth has come, and falsehood has vanished
quiz.e: Surah Bani Isra’il, verse 81; narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari on the authority of Ibn Mas‘ud (RA).

quiz.q: What is the significance of the kalimah ‘La ilaha illa Allah’ beginning with a denial?
o: First falsehood must be removed, then truth seated
First truth must be seated, then falsehood removed
Because faith is not complete without denial
Because the rule of Arabic sentence structure says so
quiz.e: First remove everything; remove the stones, remove the arrows, remove the middleman. Empty the house, then seat the One.

quiz.q: What does the sentence ‘They accepted Allah as Creator; they did not accept Him as Ruler’ mean?
o: They accepted both creation and command
They denied both creation and command
They accepted command but denied creation
They admitted creation but did not obey the command
quiz.e: They took life’s decisions by the word of the arrow placed before Hubal; that is, they did not give Allah the right of command.

quiz.q: What is the hadith’s basic principle on the limit of obedience?
o: Obedience to the leader will be unconditional and complete
There is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator
The tribe’s decision is considered final
Following society’s prevailing custom is real obedience
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 7145 and Sahih Muslim 1840; obedience is only in what is right.

quiz.q: Going to a shrine and saying ‘you put in a word for me’ repeats which Jahili argument?
o: The tribe’s leader’s word is final
Fate is decided by the spinning of arrows
The forefathers’ custom is the final proof
A ladder is needed to reach Allah
quiz.e: In Surah al-Zumar, verse 3, this very argument of the polytheists is set out exactly.

quiz.q: Looking at the newspaper horoscope before an exam is a new form of which Jahili habit?
o: Circling the Ka‘bah naked
Making vows before idols
Deciding fate by spinning arrows
Seeing good and ill omens by flying birds
quiz.e: Printed letters instead of arrows, a newspaper instead of the attendant; the hand is stretched out in the same place.

quiz.q: Siding with the party even when the party’s decision goes against Allah’s command is a form of what?
o: Changing position out of respect for idols
Taking decisions by spinning arrows
Storing up blood-vengeance
Sitting silent out of fear of poetry
quiz.e: In those days positions changed out of respect for idols; today they change to please people. The place of the test is the same.

quiz.q: With which sentence did ‘A’ishah (RA) end her account of the four kinds of marriage in the Jahili age?
o: He demolished all the marriages, except one
He kept all the marriages in place as before
He demolished all but two
He introduced a new rule of marriage
quiz.e: Hadith 5127 of Sahih al-Bukhari; all but one of the four were demolished.

quiz.q: For what purpose did the husband send his wife to another man in Nikah al-Istibda‘?
o: To pay off a debt
In the hope of a child of a hero and a great lineage
To establish peace between two tribes
To arrange food in a famine
quiz.e: The husband would say, the man is a hero, his lineage is great; if we have such a child, the honour of our house will rise.

quiz.q: In the group kind of marriage, how was the child’s paternity settled?
o: The tribal chief himself would give a verdict
Arrows would be spun before the Ka‘bah and consulted
The woman would point her finger at one man
It was settled by order of age
quiz.e: She would point at one man and say, this child is yours; and the man had to accept it.

quiz.q: In the house of open prostitution, who determined a child’s father when a child was born?
o: The owner who hung the flags
The tribe’s chief poet and soothsayer
The attendants appointed to the House of the Ka‘bah
A face-reader of the ‘Qafah’
quiz.e: He would look at the child’s face and build and say whose child it was; the man would then take the child.

quiz.q: What does the statement ‘The custom had a name; the girl’s name no one gave’ bring out?
o: The oppression was rare and exceptional
The oppression went on secretly and hidden at all times, as is generally held
The oppression had received institutional recognition
The oppression was judged and severely punished
quiz.e: It has a name, it has rules, it has society’s recognition; yet the victim has no identity.

quiz.q: Which subtle wrong did the verse Surah al-Baqarah 231 catch?
o: Holding a woman back in order to harm her
Withholding the mahr money
Divorcing without witnesses
Hiding the count of the ‘iddah
quiz.e: The man neither beat nor locked the house; he only did not release. In human courts it had no name.

quiz.q: To show the reward of one who raises two daughters, what did the Prophet ﷺ do?
o: He raised both hands towards the sky
He joined two of his own fingers to show
He stood on the pulpit and gestured
He spread the two ends of his cloak
quiz.e: Hadith 2631 of Sahih Muslim; he said, on the Day of Resurrection he and I will be like this.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the question in Surah al-Takwir being put to the girl rather than the killer?
o: On Resurrection women will be questioned first of all
The killer’s judgement has already ended
The girl too must answer for her crime
The one whom no one heard, her word will be heard
quiz.e: No one ever asked her even once what she wanted; that day the whole plain of Gathering will stand and hear her.

quiz.q: The change hidden within the statement ‘A virgin’s silence is her permission’ is
o: Even her silence is now counted
It is said that her opinion need not be taken
The guardian’s decision is made final
She is excused because of shyness
quiz.e: In a society where a girl was never asked anything, now even her silence is being heard.

porbos.title: Rights Came, and Jahiliyyah Came Back • When a Human Being Is Merchandise • Those Who Had No Name Received One • The Chain Has Been Opened, Yet • The One With No One Behind Him • The Day Allah Stood Behind the Weak • Even Today, the One With No One Behind Him • The Price of a She-Camel • Two Tribes, One Row

blocks.0: Rights Came, and Jahiliyyah Came Back
blocks.1: Now let us look at today. Today’s girl has everything that the girl of fourteen hundred years ago did not have. She has the right to give her opinion. No one can marry her off without telling her. She goes to school. She goes to college. She goes to university. She steps outside the home. She works. She keeps the money she earns in her own hands. The girl of the desert could not have imagined a single one of these. Now the question is, what are we doing with these rights?
blocks.2: A girl has come from the village to the city. Her father sold land. Her mother raises her hands in supplication after every prayer. The whole village knows that their girl studies at the university. The first few months went well. Then she met someone. First talk about class. Then talk on the phone. Then talking late into the night. The girl thought, this is nothing at all. Then sitting together. Eating together. Going about together. The girl thought, this too is nothing at all. In this way, at every step she convinced herself, this much is nothing at all. And every step carried her one step closer to the next. Satan never invites to a great sin on the very first day. He only asks you to take one small step. Then the day she had given everything, the boy said, we never said we would marry.
blocks.3: In the village the father still says proudly, my daughter studies at the university. And the mother still raises her hands after prayer. Another house. The girl has been married. She has a child. She has a husband. She goes to the office. There is a colleague there. First talk about work. Then talk that is not about work. She realises that her husband has never spoken to her like this. Her husband has been carrying the household for ten years. He leaves at dawn, returns at night. His body is tired, there is no smile on his face. And this man says every morning, you look very beautiful today. The crack begins with just this much. Then one day the household breaks apart. The child asks, where is Mummy? And there is no answer to the question.
blocks.4: In another house the breaking comes in another way. The woman earns. Sometimes more than her husband. And that money slowly becomes a weapon. At every turn she says, am I dependent on you? She says, if I were not here, would this household run? Her husband falls silent. Then small insults keep piling up. One day they pile up so high that the house is no longer a home. Islam gave woman ownership of wealth, yes. But not so that it might be made a tool for breaking the household.
blocks.5: Now step out of the house and stand on the road. At the corner a billboard. Fifty feet high. On it a picture of a girl. But the advertisement is not for her. The advertisement is for a soap. Or a mobile phone. Or steel rods. What relation does the girl have to steel rods? None. She has been placed there because sales go up when people look. That is, she herself is not the product. She is an instrument for selling the product. Such is the side of the screen. Cinema, drama, song. There a girl is acting. But the next day people do not discuss her acting. They discuss something else. And she knows it. She knows that her real job is not acting. And after that there is the trade whose name one is ashamed even to say. There is no pretence left there. There the girl is directly a commodity.
blocks.6: She can be seen. Bought. Sold. Then thrown away. And that girl too has a mother. No one remembers that. This very society shouts the slogan, woman is no commodity. And in this very society’s market the most profitable commodity is the woman’s body. One thing on the tongue. Another in the account book.
blocks.7: Now let me say the hardest thing. Where does the end of this road finally lead? Someone is used and thrown away. Someone falls into the trap of blackmail. Someone’s picture ends up in a place from where it will never be erased. And some end up in a place where their will has no value at all. Today’s boys must first look at themselves. The boy who ruins a girl’s life in the name of love, what answer will he give tomorrow on the plain of Resurrection? He too is somebody’s brother. He too will one day be somebody’s father.
blocks.8: The calculation is this. The girl of that day had no rights. So she was used. Today’s girl has rights. Yet she is being used. The difference is only one. On that day she was taken by force. Today she is persuaded. On that day the chain was put on the hand. Today the chain is put on the mind. And a chain put on the mind, people do not even recognise as a chain. She thinks, I am free.
blocks.9: Jahiliyyah has returned. But not with its old face. No one buries a girl in the ground any more. No one hangs flags on doors any more. Today’s Jahiliyyah comes in the name of freedom. It comes in the name of rights. It comes in the name of modernity. On that day people knew, this is darkness. Today people do not even know that this is darkness. And this is exactly what has made today’s Jahiliyyah harder than that day’s. The patient who knows he is ill at least looks for medicine. And the one who thinks he is well! The right was given by Allah. The Prophet {{1}} gave it with his own hands. But along with that right he had also given a limit. We took the right. We left the limit behind.
blocks.10: When a Human Being Is Merchandise
blocks.11: The fair of ‘Ukaz. Morning. In one corner a few people have been made to stand in a row. A buyer came and stood. He took one man’s face and made him open his mouth. He looked at the teeth. Then he pressed the muscles of his arm. Then he told him to walk a few steps. Exactly what people do when buying a horse. Then the bargaining began. The man is standing. His own price is being fixed in front of him. And he cannot say a single word. Because merchandise does not have the right to speak. One thing these people did not have. Lineage. In Arabia a person’s identity was in his father’s name; so-and-so, son of so-and-so. A slave was called by his owner’s name. So-and-so’s slave. That is, he is no one’s son. He is someone’s property.
blocks.12: And not everyone who stood in this market had been a slave from birth. The story is this. In a tribe towards Syria there was a boy. His father’s name was Harithah. His mother’s name was Su‘da. One day the mother took the boy to visit her parents’ home. On the way bandits fell upon them. They carried the boy off. Then they brought him to the market of ‘Ukaz and sold him. The price rose to four hundred dirhams. The boy was then eight or nine years old. In the morning he was the child of a free man. By evening he had become someone’s merchandise. And his father’s name was wiped from his name.
blocks.13: The father’s side was this. Harithah set out to search for his son. From one tribe to another. From one fair to another. No one could tell him. He composed poetry for his son, and kept reciting that poetry along the roads. I weep when the dove coos. I do not know whether he is alive or not. I only know that I keep searching. Year after year. Meanwhile the boy did not know that his father was searching for him. And the father did not know where the boy was. Two people, under the same sky. And in between, the receipt of a market.
blocks.14: And what was the worth of a slave’s life anyway? If the owner wished, he could kill him. No one would ask. Because to ask, one needs a tribe. And a slave has no tribe. When a free man was killed, a forty-year war would break out. And when a slave was killed! A piece of merchandise was spoiled, that was all.
blocks.15: Those Who Had No Name Received One
blocks.16: Do you remember that stolen boy? The one who bought him presented him as a gift to Khadijah (RA). And Khadijah gave him to her husband. Prophethood had not yet come. Some days later, in the Hajj season, a few men of the boy’s tribe came to Makkah and saw him. The news reached the father. Harithah rushed over. With him the ransom money. He said, take whatever sum is needed; only let my boy go. Muhammad {{1}} said, no money is needed. Call the boy. Whomever he chooses, with him he will go. The father was glad. Would a son stay away from his father? The boy was called. He said, I will not leave this man for anywhere. The father was stunned. He said, you are choosing slavery over freedom! The boy said, I have received from this man something I have received from no one.
blocks.17: Then Muhammad {{1}} took his hand, went and stood at the Hatim. Then he called the Quraysh and said, be witnesses; from today Zayd is free, and he is my son. Later, in Surah al-Ahzab, Allah abolished the custom of calling an adopted son by one’s own name; from then on he was again known by his own father’s name, Zayd ibn Harithah.{{2}}
blocks.19: That day a boy sold in the market of Makkah recovered a lineage. Even before prophethood. After prophethood, he first changed the language of calling. He said, do not call them ‘my slave’, ‘my slave-girl’. Say, my boy, my girl.{{1}}
blocks.20: Then he said what no one in that age had even imagined. He said, they are your brothers. So whatever you eat, feed them the same. Whatever you wear, clothe them in the same. And do not burden them with work beyond their ability.{{1}}
blocks.21: The saying did not stop there. Whatever you eat, feed them the same. Rice from the same pot. The same cloth. Then he opened the doors of freeing slaves one after another. Broke an oath! Free a slave. Broke a fast! Free a slave. Killed someone by mistake! Free a slave. And when the Qur’an described the difficult path, the very first thing it named was this too.
blocks.23: And what will make you know what the steep pass is? It is the freeing of a neck.{{1}}
blocks.24: Prayer or fasting was not set as the expiation for sins. What was set was the loosening of a person’s chain. Zayd (RA) later became a commander. And the last army that the Prophet {{1}} sent before his death, he made Zayd’s son Usamah its commander. Usamah was then about eighteen or twenty. And in that army were the senior Companions among the Muhajirun and the Ansar.{{2}}
blocks.25: Some people raised talk. The Prophet {{1}} stood on the pulpit and said, you are talking about his command! Before this you also raised talk about his father’s command. And by Allah, he was fit for command. The calculation is this. A boy sold at four hundred dirhams in the market of ‘Ukaz. His son, commander of the entire Muslim army. And standing under him are the most noble men of the Quraysh.
blocks.26: The Chain Has Been Opened, Yet
blocks.27: Today there is no slavery. Not in law. Not on paper. But inside our own homes it is like this. The person who comes in the morning and mops the house, cooks, minds the children. Where does she sit to eat at noon? At the same table as you? Or on the kitchen floor? The curry you eat, does she eat that? Or is something separate kept aside for her? Is her plate separate? The Prophet {{1}} said, whatever you eat, feed them the same. A saying from fourteen hundred years ago. And today!
blocks.28: In Jahili Arabia a person’s standing was decided by his lineage. Today it is decided by his money. In those days one who had no tribe was nobody. Today one who has no money is nobody. The measure has not changed. Only its name has. And he came and broke this very measure. The one who declared a sold boy to be his own son is our Prophet. And we are his Ummah. Tonight one thing can be done. Call the person who works in the house, sit her beside you and eat together. You will see that a Sunnah of the Prophet {{1}} has returned to your home.
blocks.29: The One With No One Behind Him
blocks.30: A house in Makkah. The man has died. He has left a son and some camels. The boy is seven. By the rule, the uncle is the guardian. The camels are now in the uncle’s pen. In the first year the uncle took one of his nephew’s fat camels, and tied a thin camel of his own in its place. The number is right, after all. The second year, another. The third year, another. No one says anything. Because there is no such thing as an account book. There is no such thing as a witness. What there is, is the uncle’s word.{{1}}
blocks.31: The boy grew up. One day he went and stood before him. He said, uncle, now hand over my father’s property. The uncle raised his face and looked. Then he said, what property! Who fed you all these years? The boy stood silent. Where would he go? Justice is held in the gathering of the tribe’s elders. And those who sit in that gathering are all this very uncle’s own people. To whom would he complain? When the one in whose hand is justice is himself the opposing party; then the wronged has nowhere else to go.
blocks.32: Now another scene. A desert road. A lone traveller. He has a few camels, some goods. On the road a few men came and surrounded him. He cried out. There were tents in the distance. There were people. No one came. Why did no one come? Because before that a question is asked. Which tribe is the man from? If the tribe is large, saving him today will be useful tomorrow. If the tribe is small, saving him today will multiply enemies tomorrow. And if he has no tribe at all! Then the calculation is easy; it is better not to go.
blocks.33: Here the real face of Arabia’s system of justice comes out. It is not that they had no justice. They did. But it was not justice of law; it was justice of fear. The more swords behind you, the greater your right. If no one is behind you, you have no right. There is an example of how far it went. In Madinah there were two Jewish tribes; Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah. The Nadir were strong. The Qurayzah weak. If anyone of the Qurayzah killed anyone of the Nadir, he had to pay with his life. And if anyone of the Nadir killed anyone of the Qurayzah! He did not have to give his life. The matter was settled with a hundred wasq of dates.{{1}}
blocks.34: The same crime. Two kinds of justice. Because one had people behind him, the other did not. Among the Arab tribes too, the same disease. Some tribes would say, two of yours for one of ours. A slave of yours will not do in place of a free man of ours. A woman of yours will not do in place of a man of ours.{{1}}
blocks.35: That is, even the price of a human life was not the same. The price was fixed by looking at lineage. And on the very bottom floor it was like this. A labourer worked all day. In the evening he stood waiting for his wages. The owner said, come tomorrow. The next day he came. The owner said, come later. He does not come any more. Because he knows that asking will do nothing; rather, the job will also be lost. His labour was taken from him, and the price was not paid. This incident was entered in no register. Because in the register of Jahiliyyah the name of the weak is not written.
blocks.36: The Day Allah Stood Behind the Weak
blocks.37: The first light fell on this darkness through a verse of the Qur’an. Allah caught the calculation of that uncle—
blocks.39: And give the orphans their property. And do not exchange the bad for the good. And do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.{{1}}
blocks.40: How subtle it is! Allah did not only say, do not steal the orphan’s property. He said, do not exchange the bad for the good. That is, the trick of keeping the number right while changing the quality was caught too. The wrong that had no name at all was given a name. Then came that verse, which makes the body tremble to hear—
blocks.42: Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only filling their bellies with fire. And soon they will enter a blazing fire.{{1}}
blocks.43: The uncle who thought no one was watching was told: it is being watched. And the account will not end in this world. After this the Qur’an pointed a finger at the whole society. In Surah al-Fajr Allah, as it were, counted the faults off one by one. You do not honour the orphan. You do not urge one another to feed the poor. You devour inheritance greedily. And you love wealth blindly.{{1}}
blocks.44: A picture of a whole society in four sentences. But the Qur’an did not stop with a rebuke. It took the weak one’s hand. And the work of taking that hand was given to one who had himself been an orphan. Allah reminded him—
blocks.46: So as for the orphan, do not oppress him. And as for the one who asks, do not scold him.{{1}}
blocks.47: The one who never saw his own father’s face, by his hand the rights of the orphan were written. And the honour he declared for the guardian of an orphan was something the Arabs had not even imagined. He said, I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this.{{1}}
blocks.48: The child who was not even allowed to stand in the tribe’s gathering, caring for him became the way to be beside the Prophet {{1}}. After this he laid his hand on the hardest place. The price of a life. Coming to Madinah he abolished that discrimination between al-Nadir and Qurayzah. Then he stated the rule; the blood of Muslims is equal. And what he joined to it was even more astonishing. He said, the protection granted by Muslims is one; even the humblest of them, if he grants protection to anyone, all must honour it.{{2}}
blocks.49: In a society where the weak one’s word had no weight, the word of the weakest person bound the whole state. On the day of the conquest of Makkah, Umm Hani (RA) gave refuge to two polytheists. ‘Ali (RA) did not want to let them go. The Prophet {{1}} said, whom you have sheltered, we too have sheltered.{{2}}
blocks.50: One woman’s single word. And above it no one else’s word ran. Then he went and stood beside that labourer. He said, Allah has said, on the Day of Resurrection I will be the adversary of three. One who makes a pledge in My name and then breaks it. One who sells a free person and eats his price. And one who hires a labourer, takes the whole work from him, yet does not pay his wages.{{1}}
blocks.51: The word is important here. Allah did not say, I will punish him. He said, I will be his adversary. That is, on one side of the case he, and on the other side Allah Himself. The labourer who had no one to stand for him, for him the Lord of the Throne stood. And he fixed the time for paying wages too. He said, pay him his wages before his sweat dries.{{1}}
blocks.52: Not tomorrow. Not later. Before the sweat dries. And lastly he made oppression itself known in such a way that after knowing it, a mistake should not be possible. He said, oppression will come as darkness on the Day of Resurrection.{{1}}
blocks.53: And the last words he said when sending Mu‘adh (RA) to Yemen are worth remembering. He said, beware the supplication of the oppressed; for there is no veil between it and Allah.{{1}}
blocks.54: The oppressed may not be able to go to anyone. But one door of his is always open. And before that door there is no guard.
blocks.55: Even Today, the One With No One Behind Him
blocks.56: Today in our society there is no tribe. There is no gathering of elders either. There are courts. There are laws. There is paper. Even so, the calculation is this. In a house the father died. He left a son, and some land. The boy is seven. The uncles said, the boy is small; we will look after the land. The statement is not false either. They truly did look after it. For twenty years.
blocks.57: The boy grew up and one day went and stood before him. The uncle raised his face and looked. Then he said, what land! Who fed you all these years? Fourteen hundred years have passed. The sentence has not changed in the least. He went to court. The law is on his side. The papers are on his side. Yet the years kept rolling. One date, then another date. The lawyer’s fees. Travel costs. The loss of working days. And on the other side the uncle has time, has money, has people. After ten years the boy counted and saw that in running the case more than the price of the land had gone. Then he stopped. Not defeated. Exhausted.
blocks.58: Now the real point. In Jahili Arabia, to get justice you needed swords behind you. Today, to get justice you need money behind you, time, people you know. For one who has not even one of these three, the law remains on paper. The condition has not changed. Only the name of the condition has. And do you remember that labourer? He is standing even today. The work is finished. Now, the money. The owner said, come next week. He came. He was told, sir is not in. The third time he did not come. Because the fare for going and coming is itself a third of what he is owed.
blocks.59: The man never came back. The owner thought, thank goodness. He does not know that the complaint has gone up. And who will be his adversary in the court of that complaint, the Prophet {{1}} said it fourteen hundred years ago. One thing we often forget. Oppression does not mean only beating. Oppression means withholding someone’s due. Oppression means not listening to someone’s word because he is weak. Oppression means delaying giving what is his. And these three things happen in our homes, and no one even calls it oppression.
blocks.60: The one who set a common woman’s grant of refuge above the decision of a whole state is our Prophet. And we are his Ummah. So take two works from today’s lesson. One, if anyone’s due is held back in your hand, give it today. However small. Two, if among your relatives some orphan’s right is held back in someone’s hand, at least raise the matter. Speaking a word for the oppressed is also a work. Because standing behind the one who has no one behind him is the greatest Sunnah.
blocks.62: A pasture. On the grass a she-camel is grazing. Her name is Sarab. She belongs to an old woman named al-Basus. Grazing, she mistakenly strayed into the neighbouring tribe’s boundary. Far off stood the leader of that tribe, Kulayb. He raised his bow. The arrow went and pierced the she-camel’s udder. Milk flowed with blood onto the ground. The she-camel limped back to the front of the tent. Al-Basus came out and saw. Then she cried out— my humiliation! my humiliation! That one cry was enough. That very day a young man of her tribe went and killed Kulayb. Then Kulayb’s tribe took revenge. Then revenge again. Then again.
blocks.63: That war lasted forty years. What does forty years mean? Those who had started the war grew old and died. Their sons fought. When the sons died, the grandsons fought. The child born in the first year of the war grew up and fought in the war, married, and had a son. That son too grew up and went to the very same war. Toward the end many could no longer even remember what it had started over. A she-camel’s udder. Its price was paid with thousands upon thousands of lives of two tribes.
blocks.64: Another war was called Dahis and Ghabra’. The names of two horses. A wager on a horse race had been made between two tribes. During the race one side put men on the road and blocked the other side’s horse. From this, quarrelling. Then scuffling. Then blood. That blood stopped after several decades.{{1}}
blocks.65: The causes together are like this. A she-camel crossed a boundary. Someone cheated in a horse race. Someone said a bitter word about someone’s tribe. Someone’s camel drank from someone’s well. This much was enough. To kill people they needed no great cause. And more terrible than this was the second side. They did not forget this blood. The wars did not run continuously. In between, years upon years passed in silence. But the enmity did not die. It was stored up inside the home. The tent at night. By the fire, a five-year-old boy in his father’s lap. The first lesson, genealogy. The second lesson, the account of blood. Banu so-and-so killed three of ours. Your grandfather’s blood has still not been avenged. The child is reciting it all in a lisping voice. No one has told him where he came from. No one has told him where he will go. No one has taught him the name of Allah.
blocks.66: But he knows, Banu so-and-so are our enemies. The revenge for one blood would be stored up for three or four generations. No one forgot. No one forgave either. The reason lay within their system. A tribe that could not take revenge, the poets wrote satirical verse about them. That verse spread from mouth to mouth. And lived on, generation after generation. To forgive meant lasting disgrace. So they had no way except to take revenge. With one killing was born the next killing. And with it the one after. The chain stopped nowhere.
blocks.68: In Madinah there were two tribes. Aws and Khazraj. Their enmity was a hundred and twenty years old.{{1}}
blocks.69: The last war was called Bu‘ath. The blood of that war had not yet dried. The Prophet {{1}} came to Madinah. Within a few years, the people of those two tribes were standing in one row to pray. Standing beside the man who had killed his father. Shoulder to shoulder. Allah preserved that event in the Qur’an.
blocks.71: And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies of one another; then He joined your hearts, and by His grace you became brothers.{{1}}
blocks.72: Allah did not say, I stopped their war. He said, I put affection in the hearts. Stopping a war is easy. For that a strong ruler is enough. But wiping out a hundred and twenty years of hatred! That is not a ruler’s work. Then came the day of the Farewell Hajj. The plain of ‘Arafah. Before him more than a hundred thousand people. Almost every one of these people had an account of blood stored up at home. Someone’s father had been killed. Someone’s brother. Someone’s son. He declared, all blood-vengeance of Jahiliyyah is cancelled from today. All. The account of four generations of a whole people was wiped out in one sentence. But he did not stop here. He said, and the first blood I forgive is that of my own clan. The blood of the infant son of Rabi‘ah ibn al-Harith.{{1}}
blocks.73: He did not ask others to forgive. He began with the blood of his own house. After this no one has anything left to say. And the greatest change came in ‘asabiyyah. Above the tribe, which had been the only identity, he set taqwa. In that same sermon he said— there is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab. Nor of a non-Arab over an Arab. Nor of the white over the black. Nor of the black over the white. Superiority is only in taqwa. And the Qur’an stated the reason.
blocks.75: O mankind! I created you from one male and one female; and I made you into different nations and tribes, so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most honoured among you in the sight of Allah is the one who has the most taqwa.{{1}}
blocks.76: Tribes will remain. But a tribe is only a name of identity. Not a measure of honour. So beside the son of a chief of Makkah stood the Abyssinian slave Bilal. And on the day the time came to climb the roof of the Ka‘bah and call the adhan, he called Bilal. Those on whose chests a stone had once been laid, their voice that day flowed over the whole of Makkah.
