quiz.q: How did the lesson view informing a girl of her marriage without taking her consent?
o: Her silence is full consent
Her silence is not permission, but fear
Her silence is an expression of shyness
Her silence is part of an age-old custom
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said that silence is permission; but that silence was free, not out of fear.

quiz.q: What is the lesson’s assessment of using a woman’s picture in an advertisement for steel rods?
o: She is a partner of the advertising firm
She herself is a commodity being sold
She is not the commodity, but an instrument for selling the commodity
She is an independent bearer of publicity
quiz.e: She has no relation to the rods; she is placed there because sales go up when people look.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of ‘On that day the chain was put on the hand, today it is put on the mind’?
o: There are no chains anywhere now
The prisoner understands his own imprisonment
The free person thinks himself imprisoned
The prisoner learns to think himself free
quiz.e: A chain put on the mind, people do not even recognise as a chain; she thinks, I am free.

quiz.q: How did Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) fall into slavery?
o: Sold in place of his father’s debt
Captured as a prisoner in a tribal war
Falling into the hands of bandits on the road with his mother
By birth, in the house of a slave mother
quiz.e: Kidnapped at the age of eight or nine, he was sold in the market of ‘Ukaz for four hundred dirhams.

quiz.q: What was revealed by the custom of calling a slave by his owner’s name instead of his father’s name?
o: He is an honoured member of the tribe
He is no one’s son, he is someone’s property
He is an adopted child of the owner’s house
He is a person held captive temporarily
quiz.e: In Arabia identity was in the father’s name; a slave was called by his owner’s name.

quiz.q: Which instruction about slaves came in the hadith narrated by Abu Dharr (RA)?
o: Double their wages right now
Make a separate arrangement for their lodging
Reduce their working hours
Feed them what you eat, clothe them in what you wear
quiz.e: Hadith 30 of Sahih al-Bukhari; he said, they are your brothers.

quiz.q: In describing the ‘steep pass’ in Surah al-Balad, which deed came first?
o: Freeing a neck
Feeding an orphan on a day of hunger
Giving shelter to a close-kin orphan
Counselling one another to patience
quiz.e: Not prayer or fasting even as expiation for sins; what was set was the loosening of a person’s chain.

quiz.q: What is the significance of setting the freeing of a slave, instead of prayer or fasting, as expiation for sins?
o: To make the rule of expiation easier, as is generally held
To show the importance of worship as less
To give priority to a person’s freedom
To bring down the wealth in the hands of the rich
quiz.e: As the remedy for sin, what was set was the loosening of a person’s chain.

quiz.q: What action is given at the end of the lesson regarding the person who works in the home?
o: To sit her beside you and eat together
To raise her salary
To reduce her working hours
To give her a separate room
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, whatever you eat, feed them the same; rice from the same pot, the same cloth.

quiz.q: ‘Today one who has no money is nobody’: this is a new face of which Jahili principle?
o: Having a sword means being a hero
No tribe means he is nobody
Having a poet means the tribe is strong
A great lineage means he is honoured
quiz.e: In those days standing was decided by lineage; today it is decided by money.

quiz.q: The discrimination in blood-price between Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah was
o: The blood-price of both tribes was equal
If one of the Nadir killed, it was settled with a hundred wasq of dates
If one of the Qurayzah killed, only a fine had to be paid
Both tribes left the matter to a judge; this is how it is generally held
quiz.e: Hadith 4494 of Sunan Abi Dawud; if one of the Qurayzah killed, he had to pay with his life.

quiz.q: What was the real condition for getting justice in Jahili Arabia, according to the lesson?
o: Being close to the tribal chief; this is how it is generally held
Being able to present witnesses and proof
How many swords were behind you decided the size of your right
Being willing to take an oath before the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: They had justice, but not the justice of law; the justice of fear.

quiz.q: What did Allah say in the hadith qudsi about the labourer’s wages?
o: I will give him severe punishment
I will not accept his deeds
On the Day of Resurrection I will be his adversary
I will constrict his provision; this is how it is generally held
quiz.e: Hadith 2270 of Sahih al-Bukhari; among the three is the one who hires a labourer, takes the whole work, and does not pay the wages.

quiz.q: What is the subtlety of saying ‘do not exchange the bad for the good’ in Surah al-Nisa’, verse 2?
o: The orphan’s property must not be touched at all; this is how it is generally held
The trick of keeping the number right while changing the quality was caught too
The orphan’s property may be divided
The guardian has no remuneration
quiz.e: The wrong that had no name at all was given a name.

quiz.q: How does the lesson show the significance of ‘the protection granted by Muslims is one’?
o: Only the head of state can grant protection
Protection must be granted with the tribal chief’s permission; this is how it is generally held
Consultation is necessary before granting protection
The word of the weakest person bound the whole state
quiz.e: On the day of the conquest of Makkah the Prophet ﷺ upheld the refuge given by Umm Hani’ (RA).

quiz.q: What is the Prophet’s ﷺ warning to Mu‘adh (RA) regarding the supplication of the oppressed?
o: There is no veil between it and Allah
His supplication is accepted within three days
His supplication is accepted only at night
By his supplication the wealth of the oppressor is destroyed
quiz.e: Hadith 1496 of Sahih al-Bukhari; even if the oppressed cannot go to anyone, one door of his is always open.

quiz.q: On withholding someone’s due, the definition of oppression this lesson gives is
o: Oppression means only physical harm
Withholding a due, not listening to a word, and delaying giving are oppression too
Oppression is possible only for the powerful
It is oppression only if proved in court
quiz.e: And these three things happen in our homes, yet no one even calls it oppression.

quiz.q: What is the significance of ‘He put affection in the hearts’ in Surah Al ‘Imran?
o: The natural result of weariness from a long war
The result of a strong ruler’s firm hand
The result of a written agreement between the two sides
Not outside pressure, but inner change
quiz.e: To stop a war a strong ruler is enough; but wiping out a hundred and twenty years of hatred is not.

quiz.q: What is the significance of beginning with his own clan both in the blood-vengeance and in the usury at the Farewell Hajj?
o: Reform begins from one’s own home
His own clan’s account was the greatest
Because others’ accounts would be dealt with later
Because the people of the clan had raised objections
quiz.e: He did not ask others to forgive; he began with the blood of his own house and the usury of his own uncle.

porbos.title: The Tribe Is Gone, the Party Has Come • The Blood That Now Is Shed in the Name of the Party • The Cup, the Arrow and the Account Book • The Day Wine Flowed Through the Alleys of Madinah • The Name Has Changed, the Deed Has Not • The Youth That Had No Task • Those Very Youths He Transformed • The Night Is Gone, and Nothing Is Remembered

blocks.0: The Tribe Is Gone, the Party Has Come
blocks.1: Today no one fights for a she-camel. But in a village a case between two families has been going on for thirty years. It began over the ridge of a boundary. Those who began it are in their graves. Now their sons are fighting. Several times the price of the land has been spent on lawyers. Still no one stops. Because if they stop, people will say, they lost. The same old calculation. To forgive is to be disgraced.
blocks.2: The tribe has gone. But the thing has not gone; it has only taken a new name. Today it is the party. Today it is the opinion. Today it is the locality, the region, the language. And the saddest place is that today it has entered even the mosque. Two sides over the committee chair. Two sides over the imam. Two sides over a tiny difference on a ruling. And the quarrel goes so far that the two sides build separate mosques. The house meant to make people stand in one row is itself divided. Aws and Khazraj were able to stand in one row. And we!
blocks.3: Jahili ‘asabiyyah has a simple description. It is this: my people are right; everyone else is wrong. Even if a man of my party does wrong, I am on his side. Even if a man of another party does good, I am against him. This very question came before the Prophet {{1}}. He said, help your brother; whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. The Companions asked in astonishment, we understand helping the oppressed; but how are we to help the oppressor? He said, by holding him back from oppression.{{2}}
blocks.4: The answer is the real point here. To help your own man does not mean to approve his wrongdoing. To help your own man means to catch his hand. In this single sentence the back of Jahili ‘asabiyyah was broken. On that day for a she-camel blood was shed for forty years. Today for a word two brothers have not spoken for thirty years. On that day poets wrote satirical verse. Today it is written in a Facebook post. On that day the call went out in the name of the tribe. Today in the name of the party. The cause has not changed. Only the face has changed. The one who made a hundred and twenty years of enmity stand in one row is our Prophet. And we are his Ummah. With whom have I not spoken, and for how long! And is that silence truly for some reason that big?
blocks.5: The Blood That Now Is Shed in the Name of the Party
blocks.6: On that day the question was, which tribe are you from? Today the question is, which party are you from? The question has changed. What happens when the answer does not fit has not changed. One procession is going. Another procession is coming from the opposite side. In the middle a crossroads. First slogans. Then bricks. Then something sharp. In the evening a mother sits in a hospital corridor. Inside, her son lies. Age nineteen.
blocks.7: No one knew the boy. The one who struck him did not know him either. There was no quarrel between the two. No debt. Only one wore cloth of one colour, and the other cloth of another colour. That was all. On that day, over the grazing of a she-camel, blood was shed between two tribes for forty years. No one asked who the man was. They asked, which tribe is he from. Even today no one asks who the man is. They ask, which party is he from. The name has changed. The colour of the blood has not.
blocks.8: And this is the most frightening thing. The Arab of that day knew he was taking revenge. He knew the act was settling an account of blood. Today a person thinks he is fighting on the side of justice. He thinks, if the party survives the country will survive. So he does not count taking a life as anything very great. Jahiliyyah is most dangerous exactly when it begins to think of itself as justice.
blocks.9: The Prophet {{1}} shut this door completely. Standing on the plain of the Farewell Hajj he said—
blocks.11: Indeed your blood, your property and your honour are sacred to you; as sacred as this day of yours, this month of yours and this city of yours.{{1}}
blocks.12: What did he compare it with? The day of ‘Arafah. The month of Dhu al-Hijjah. The city of Makkah. To the Arabs nothing was more sacred than these. He said, a Muslim’s blood is exactly that sacred. And he also said the thing that ought to remain lodged in all our chests. He said, abusing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.{{1}}
blocks.13: He also said, after me do not become like disbelievers, striking one another’s necks with the sword.{{1}}
blocks.14: And in which register this act is written, he has told us that too. He said, whoever fights under a blind banner, gets angry out of attachment to the party, leaps up at the party’s call, and dies in that state; his death is a Jahili death.{{1}}
blocks.15: The saying is hard. He may pray. He may fast. Yet his death is a Jahili death. Because the cause for which he died is itself the cause of Jahiliyyah. And the Qur’an has made the account clear.
blocks.17: And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell; he will abide in it forever. And Allah has become angry with him, has cursed him, and has prepared for him a great punishment.{{1}}
blocks.18: Four punishments in one verse. Hell, abiding forever, wrath, curse. There are not many such verses in the Qur’an. Now the last word. About that boy of the procession. For whom did he die? The leader for whom he died did not go to the hospital. After a few days a message of condolence came. Then everything was over. And the mother still goes every night, opens the door of her son’s room, and looks once.
blocks.19: The one who, standing before more than a hundred thousand people on the plain of ‘Arafah, wiped out the account of blood of four generations in one sentence, is our Prophet. And we shed blood for a crossroads.
blocks.20: The Cup, the Arrow and the Account Book
blocks.21: A house. Night has fallen. Lamps are burning. A carpet is spread. The cup passes from hand to hand. In one corner the gambling arrows are being shaken. Drunk, one man stood up. Then he gave away his whole herd of camels. Everyone clapped. The next morning he will remember nothing. But the whole tribe will remember. And the poet will write verse about it.
blocks.22: Wine was not a shame to them. It was a pride. Because squandering wealth after drinking was also a proof of generosity. The matter had entered even their language. They named the grapevine ‘karm’. That is, nobility. The poet ‘Antarah proudly wrote in his Mu‘allaqah, when I drink I squander my wealth.{{1}}
blocks.23: Pride in intoxication in a people’s finest poetry. The standard can be understood from this. And you will be astonished to hear what their gambling was like. A camel would be brought. Then it was slaughtered and divided into several shares. Then arrows were drawn. On some arrows a share was written. Some arrows were blank. Those whose arrows came up blank had to pay the whole price of the camel.{{1}}
blocks.24: And they did not get even a piece of the meat. Here is the real point. The meat that was divided, they did not eat it themselves. They gave it away to the poor. So they did not call it gambling. They called it charity. They called it generosity. A whole people gambling, and thinking they were doing a righteous deed. Another house. Inside sits a man. Account papers in his hand. Last year he had borrowed ten. He could not repay. So it became twenty. This year too he could not. So it became forty. He had not spent a single coin more. Only time had passed. The creditor came and stood at the door. First the deed of the land went. Then the deed of the house. Then nothing was left. At last he took the boy’s hand and placed it in the creditor’s hand. A free man became a slave that day.
blocks.25: Without any war. Only on a sheet of account paper.
blocks.26: The Day Wine Flowed Through the Alleys of Madinah
blocks.27: Wine was not made unlawful in a single day. A habit so old cannot be torn out in one pull. So Allah proceeded step by step. In the first step He only showed the account.
blocks.29: They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, in both is great sin, and some benefits for people; but their sin is greater than their benefit.{{1}}
blocks.30: The benefit is there, it was admitted. But work out the calculation. In the second step the time was restricted.
blocks.32: O believers! Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated.{{1}}
blocks.33: Five prayers a day. So there was almost no time left for wine. Then in the third step the final word came down.
blocks.35: O believers! Wine, gambling, altars for idols and divining arrows; these are but the work of Satan, filthy things. So avoid them.{{1}}
blocks.36: The verse was revealed. A herald set out to call through the alleys of Madinah. Wine has become unlawful. Anas (RA) says, that day he was serving wine in Abu Talhah’s house. A vessel in his hand. People sitting in the gathering. The call reached his ears. Abu Talhah said, go out and pour it away. Anas went out and poured it out.{{1}}
blocks.37: That day wine flowed through the alleys of Madinah. Someone had the cup at his lips; he threw it down. Someone had a jar full in his house; he smashed it. No one said, let me finish today’s and give it up from tomorrow. At the end of the verse Allah had asked, will you then desist? And they answered, we have desisted.{{1}}
blocks.38: One question. One answer. And the habit of centuries of a whole people ended in one evening. And regarding gambling Allah did not stop at saying it is unlawful. He told the reason too.
blocks.40: Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to keep you from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer.{{1}}
blocks.41: The harm is not only of money. The harm is of relationships. At the gambling table one wins, another loses. And the one who loses does not rise with a smile. Something keeps piling up inside him. And the second harm is greater still. Keeping from prayer. Because the man who has sat up all night, where does his Fajr time go?
blocks.42: In the Qur’an Allah has spoken of many sins. But for one sin He used a word He used nowhere else. War.
blocks.44: And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.{{1}}
blocks.45: A war by his Lord against a servant. And He did not seize only the one who eats it. The Prophet {{1}} said, the one who eats usury, the one who gives it, the one who writes it, and the one who witnesses it; all are equal.{{2}}
blocks.46: As many people as it takes to keep the business going, all of them. Then came the day of the Farewell Hajj. He declared, all usury of Jahiliyyah is cancelled from today. And the first I cancel is what is owed to my own uncle ‘Abbas.{{1}}
blocks.47: He did not ask others to let go. He began with his own house. And when usury stops, where will the poor man get money? So he established zakah. And the Qur’an did not call zakah charity.
blocks.49: And in their wealth is a known right; for the one who asks and the deprived.{{1}}
blocks.50: A right. When the rich give it, he is not being kind. He is returning someone else’s due.
blocks.51: The Name Has Changed, the Deed Has Not
blocks.52: Today no cup goes around in our homes. But the intoxication has remained. Only the names have changed. And one thing has increased. On that day the old and the young took intoxicants. Today the boys of schools and colleges do. And the argument is ready. All the friends do it. Just once. It eases tension. The man of Jahili Arabia said exactly this too. He said, there is some benefit in it. And the Qur’an accepted his statement and answered. There is benefit, right. But the sin is greater than the benefit.
blocks.53: And those gambling arrows! They no longer stay in the quiver. Now they stay inside the phone. The game starts. The boy puts money on the phone. If he wins, he stakes more. If he loses, he thinks, next time I’ll get it back. And in exactly this way a household is finished. He too tells himself, this is not gambling. It’s just a little entertainment. The man of Jahili Arabia too told himself, this is not gambling; this is charity. The name has changed. The deed has not.
blocks.54: That account paper is there too. Only now it stays in the bank’s ledger. And the name is no longer usury. Now it is profit. It is service charge. It is rate of return. And the end is the same. Land is sold. Then the tin of the roof. Then the housewife’s earring. Then one day the man flees the village. On that day the boy had to be handed over. Today one’s own homestead. And usury is not only in the bank. In the village one man lends another ten thousand. The condition is, at month’s end you must give twelve. No one calls this usury. They say, I kept a little profit. Both of them pray. And both are in that list where four are named.
blocks.55: Allah placed wine, gambling and idols in the same verse. Why? Because the disease inside the three is one. People want results without effort. From the idol they want blessing without deeds. From the gambling arrow they want money without labour. And in the usury ledger they want profit without trade. All three are the same door. The door of getting it easily. And on that day wine flowed through the alleys of Madinah. Not one of them asked for even a single day. They said, we have desisted. Today the same question is placed before us too. Will you then desist?
blocks.56: The Youth That Had No Task
blocks.57: The greatest poet of Jahili Arabia was named Imru’ al-Qays. A prince of the Kindah tribe. But the boy did not sit in the royal court. He wrote poetry, drank wine, and roamed the desert with his friends. At last his father drove him from the house. Then one day news came that Banu Asad had killed his father. When the news came, the cup was in his hand. He did not put the cup down. He said, today wine, tomorrow the task. Then he ran for the rest of his life. From one tribe to another, finally to the court of the Roman emperor. On the way back near Ankara he fell ill and died right there. The revenge was not taken. The kingdom did not come back. The greatest poet of Arabia, and his grave is not even in the soil of Arabia.{{1}}
blocks.58: The man had no lack of intelligence. No lack of courage. No lack of wealth either. What he lacked was a purpose. And without purpose, however great the strength, it only keeps burning. Now leave the prince and come to the youth of the whole people. Where their time went can be understood through a few scenes.
blocks.59: First scene. The greatest intoxication of Jahili Arabia was not wine. Its name was pride. And the subject of pride was only one; lineage. The youths of two tribes have sat facing each other. The question is only one; who is greater. One stood up and began to count the names of his lineage. Father, grandfather, grandfather’s father. Another stood and counted. Then began the counting of people; how many houses we have, how many you have. Whoever’s number was greater, that day he was the greater.
blocks.60: That this game had truly entered their blood, the Prophet {{1}} himself said. He said, four habits of Jahiliyyah will remain even in my Ummah; they will not give them up. Boasting about lineage. Taunting others about their lineage. Asking for rain through the stars. And wailing for the dead.{{2}}
blocks.61: Two of the four are about lineage. And the Qur’an gave this very contest its name—
blocks.63: Competition in abundance has distracted you; until you reach the graves.{{1}}
blocks.64: That is, this counting did not stop until death came. A whole life passed matching numbers. And not one of those numbers went with them into the grave. Second scene. A boy is ten. One day the uncle called him and made him sit beside him. Then he raised his finger towards a tribe far off and said, those there; they owe us blood. They killed your grandfather. Remember.
blocks.65: The boy grew up carrying this word in his chest. He did not see the beginning of the war. He does not know the reason either. He only knows that the hatred is his. Do you remember that forty-year war? The boy who was born in the twentieth year of that war, his whole youth passed settling the account of a she-camel. He never saw the she-camel. He never saw the one who shot the arrow either. Even so his sword is bound to that account.
blocks.66: Third scene. A young man has been thrown out of the tribe. The reason may be a quarrel, a crime, or merely his mother’s identity. Now he has no tribe. No tribe means no food, no safety, no identity. What does he do then? He forms a band with a few others like him. Then they sit by the road. When a caravan comes they leap upon it. This is how they eat. This is how they live.{{1}}
blocks.67: And the strangest thing is this. Even this banditry was not a shame to them. They wrote poems about it. Who had gone how many nights without food, who could run fastest, who had brought down how big a caravan. A whole youth spent in banditry. And poems written in pride of that youth.
blocks.68: Fourth scene. A house in one corner of the city. A flag on the door. Inside, singing. A young man went the first night out of curiosity. Then he went out of habit. In the first month one camel went. Then another. Before the year had turned, the herd his father left was finished. Then the land. Then nothing was left.{{1}}
blocks.69: The people of the tribe whispered, the boy has been ruined. But no one took his hand. Because to take it they would have had to say, the act is wrong. And to say wrong you need a measure. That very measure they did not have. The last scene is the most ordinary. A boy’s day begins at noon; the night was spent at the gathering. In the afternoon the poets’ gathering in the market. Some sing the virtues of their own tribe, some abuse another tribe. The youths clap. And that very abuse, a few months later, becomes the cause of a war.{{1}}
blocks.70: In this way twenty years pass. Thirty years pass. Then one day in a small quarrel someone drives a spear into his chest. The tribe brings back the body. The poet writes an elegy. A few days of weeping. Then everything is over. The calculation is this. Winning by counting the dead. Finishing one’s youth taking revenge for blood never seen. Sitting by the road to plunder caravans and boasting of it. Squandering in the house of song the wealth the father left. The youth of this people lacked nothing. They had intelligence, courage, language, lineage. What they lacked was only the answer to one question. Why have I come?
blocks.72: A young man is walking in an alley of Makkah. After he has passed, the fragrance stays in the alley. His name is Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr. His mother is wealthy. No want in the house. His clothes come from Yemen. The mothers of Makkah tell their sons, be like Mus‘ab.{{1}}
blocks.73: Then one day he entered the house of al-Arqam. And when he came out, he was a Muslim. He kept the matter secret. But it did not stay secret. His mother got the news. She kept her son locked in the house. She stopped his food. She thought, in two days the boy will come back. A boy who has never suffered a single hardship in life, how long can he last?
blocks.74: He lasted. One day he got a chance and left the house. The boy whose clothes used to come from Yemen now wore a patched cloak. The Companions, seeing him, would lower their heads. So that no one would see the tears. But I have not yet said the real thing. Whom did the Prophet {{1}} send to teach the Qur’an in Madinah? Not some elder. He sent this young man.{{2}}
blocks.75: Going to Madinah he did only one thing. He went from house to house and sat. He recited the Qur’an to them. One day Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh came charging with a spear in hand. He was then the chief of a tribe of Madinah, and still a polytheist. Mus‘ab said quietly, please sit. Listen. If you do not like it, you may go. He sat. And when he rose, he was a Muslim. Before that evening his whole tribe had accepted Islam.{{1}}
blocks.76: Before the Prophet {{1}} reached Madinah the city had been made ready. By the hand of one young man. Then came the day of Uhud. The banner was in his hand. There he was martyred. When they came to shroud him, the Companions were stunned. The cloth was so short that if the head was covered the feet showed, and if the feet were covered the head. The Prophet {{2}} said, cover the head; and put idhkhir grass over the feet.{{3}}
blocks.77: Just once place two pictures side by side. The young man in the alley of Makkah whose fragrance lingered. And the one on the field of Uhud whose shroud did not cover his whole body. What happened in between? Nothing. Only a purpose for life had been found. And Mus‘ab was not alone. Most of the small group that sat hidden in the house of al-Arqam were under thirty. ‘Ali (RA) accepted Islam at the age of ten. Al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam and Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) were then just past boyhood, barely young men.{{1}}
blocks.78: The first caravan of Islam was a caravan of youths. On the day of Uhud a boy came and stood in the line. Age fourteen. The Prophet {{1}} looked at him and sent him back; too young. The boy went back. The next year, on the day of the Trench, he came and stood again. This time he stood on tiptoe, as tall as he could. This time permission was granted.{{2}}
blocks.79: He waited a whole year. Only to stand in the line. And on the field of Badr, a few boys. Mu‘adh ibn ‘Amr ibn al-Jamuh. And Afra’s two sons; Mu‘adh ibn Afra’ and Mu‘awwidh ibn Afra’. The matter of Afra’ (RA) is separate. In history she is called Umm al-Shuhada’; mother of the martyrs. Seven sons. In the houses of two husbands. And all seven that day stood on the field of Badr.
blocks.80: What happened afterwards did not happen in one day. Some were martyred at Badr itself. Some on the day of al-Raji‘. Some at Bi’r Ma‘unah. Some on the field of Yamamah. One house, and its sons scattered across field after field. Each time the mother received the news. And each time she remained standing.{{1}}
blocks.81: Two of them were standing that day on either side of ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA). He himself said later, I was thinking then that standing between these two I was not safe. Suddenly one of them asked quietly, uncle, which one is Abu Jahl? He said in astonishment, what do you want with him? They said, we have heard he abuses the Prophet {{1}}. By Allah, if I see him I will not let him go. Then they leapt like falcons.{{2}}
blocks.82: Abu Jahl fell to the ground that day at the hands of these very boys. And some of Afra’s sons never returned from that field. At the age when boys are on the playing field, they wrote history. The full account of Badr will come in its own place; that discussion is in the lesson on Badr. Here just see this much, that day the youngest were at the very front.
blocks.83: Let me tell of one more boy. Zayd ibn Thabit. On the day of Badr he too had the wish. His age was then thirteen. He too was sent back. But another task was waiting for him. The Prophet {{1}} called him and said, learn the writing of the Jews; I cannot be at ease about their letters. He sat down to learn. Within a few weeks he mastered the language.{{2}}
blocks.84: Then he became the chief scribe of revelation. And the story does not end there. After the passing of the Prophet {{1}}, in the battle of Yamamah many hafiz were martyred. ‘Umar (RA) rushed to Abu Bakr (RA); the Qur’an must be gathered in one place. The decision was made. Now the question, to whom would the task be given? The greatest responsibility of the Ummah.
blocks.85: The one Abu Bakr (RA) called was that very boy. He said, you are a young man, an intelligent man; and we have no suspicion about you.{{1}}
blocks.86: The boy who had once been told, you are small; do not stand in the line. By that very boy’s hand the whole Qur’an came between one pair of covers. And one more thing. These youths he did not merely put to work. He gave them honour. On the Day of Resurrection, the seven whom Allah will place in the shade of His Throne, who is one of them? The young man who has grown up in the worship of Allah.{{1}}
blocks.87: In the list, a just ruler. And right after him, a young man. On the Day of Resurrection every person will be asked five questions. Where did you end your life. What did you do with your knowledge. Where did you earn your wealth, and where did you spend it. And one question separately. Where did you wear away your youth.{{1}}
blocks.88: There is the account of life, of course. Even so, the account of youth will be asked separately. Because what is most precious, its account is separate too.
blocks.89: The Night Is Gone, and Nothing Is Remembered
blocks.90: Today our boy does not sit in a gathering of wine. He does not shake the gambling arrows. He does not go to the poets’ gathering either. Even so, the calculation is this. One o’clock at night. The room’s light is off. By the pillow the phone glows. One video ends, another begins. He had decided he would watch for ten minutes. Three hours have passed. Ask him what he watched and he cannot say. He remembers nothing. Only the night is gone.
blocks.91: The adhan of Fajr is called. He hears it. Then he turns over and sleeps. He wakes at eleven. Head heavy. Temper bad. And the day is over before it begins. The youth of that day had to walk all the way to the house with the flag. Today the house itself is in the pocket. On that day there was no shame, so the door stood open. Today there is shame, so the door is kept shut. But the deed is the same. And the loss is greater. Because he knew he was doing wrong. And our boy does not even know when he lost what.
blocks.92: And his aim! The very same. What will people say. On that day a name would come up in the poet’s verse. Today a like falls on a post. On that day the tribe clapped. Today a few hundred strangers. The urge is the same. Only the stage has changed. So is everything finished? No. Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr did not come from some separate world. He grew up in the very same alley of Makkah where the night gatherings were held. ‘Ali, al-Zubayr, Sa‘d; none of them were men of some different soil. They were children of this very Jahiliyyah. Imru’ al-Qays had intelligence, had courage, had wealth; he had no purpose. And Mus‘ab had that very purpose.
blocks.93: So where did the change happen? One man told them, your life has a purpose. You did not come just like that. One day you will be asked. And that single saying was enough. The young man who knows he will have to give an account, his night is no longer wasted. So take one task from today’s lesson. Nothing big. Tonight sleep with the phone outside the bed. And on hearing the Fajr adhan, stand up once. Just once. The change begins from there.

94.title: Practical Resolve
94.text: Jahiliyyah did not leave with the idols. It stayed in the house as habit. Today I will ask myself one question: which habit in my home is really of Jahiliyyah, with only its name changed? Today I will give up one of them, and put a Sunnah in its place, which from today on I will not leave.

The words of the hadith: the first to come to us were Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum (RA); they used to teach people the Qur’an. That is, the first two to arrive in Madinah. The account of sending Mus‘ab (RA) in particular as teacher and caller appears in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and Ibn Sa‘d’s Tabaqat.

In the house of her first husband, al-Harith ibn Rifa‘ah: Mu‘adh, Mu‘awwidh and ‘Awf; in the house of her second husband, Bukayr ibn Yalil al-Laythi: Iyas, ‘Aqil, Khalid and ‘Amir. All seven sons took part in Badr. The account of their martyrdom: at Badr (who they were is a matter of differing reports; in some Mu‘adh and Mu‘awwidh, in others Mu‘awwidh, ‘Awf and ‘Aqil), Khalid on the day of al-Raji‘, ‘Amir at Bi’r Ma‘unah, Iyas at Yamamah. See Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah; Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab. In modern writing her house is also called ‘Madrasat al-Shuhada’’; that is a descriptive epithet, not a historical title.

Three sons of Afra’ (RA), Mu‘adh, Mu‘awwidh and ‘Awf, took part in Badr; it is reported that all seven of her children were on the field that day. Mu‘awwidh and ‘Awf (RA) were martyred at Badr itself, and one hand of Mu‘adh ibn ‘Amr (RA) was cut off that day. The wounded Abu Jahl was finally killed by ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (RA); Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3962. The difference of report is about the names, not about the event.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ mean by ‘help the oppressor brother too’?
o: Keeping his crime hidden
Standing by him in his wrongdoing
Taking his hand and turning him back from oppression
Becoming a witness in his favour
quiz.e: Hadith 2444 of Sahih al-Bukhari; in reply to the Companions’ question he said, by holding him back from oppression.

quiz.q: If, in a quarrel over the mosque committee, the two sides build separate mosques, what is that a sign of?
o: A lack of leadership has become plain
The number of people has grown
Differences over rulings have greatly increased
Tribal partisanship has taken a new name
quiz.e: Aws and Khazraj were able to stand in one row; the house meant to unite is itself being divided.

quiz.q: What is the reason for calling party bloodshed even more dangerous than Jahili bloodshed?
o: Today weapons have become far more fearsome
Today the number of dead is many times greater
Today a person thinks he is fighting on the side of justice
Today there is no way at all to get justice
quiz.e: The Arab of that day knew he was taking revenge; Jahiliyyah is most dangerous exactly when it begins to think of itself as justice.

quiz.q: In giving away the gambling meat to the poor, what was the greatest danger?
o: The poor would become used to getting meat
They would think sin to be a righteous deed
The number of camels would quickly decline
The debt of the losing man would increase
quiz.e: So they did not call it gambling, they called it charity; a whole people gambling and thinking it is earning reward.

quiz.q: To give charity yet not think about the source of that money; which example is this like?
o: Those who made the pact of Hilf al-Fudul
Sa‘sa‘ah’s buying girls with camels
Abu Bakr’s (RA) freeing of slaves
The charity of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an
quiz.e: Hadith 214 of Sahih Muslim; he used to give charity, yet the Prophet ﷺ said that none of it would avail him.

quiz.q: At the Farewell Hajj, in the declaration cancelling usury, whose usury did the Prophet ﷺ cancel first?
o: The account of usury owed to Abu Sufyan
The usury owed to his own uncle ‘Abbas
What was owed to ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an
The money owed to al-‘As ibn Wa’il
quiz.e: He did not ask others to let go; he began with the account of his own house.

quiz.q: On the day the announcement making wine unlawful came, what was Anas (RA) doing?
o: Doing business in the market of Madinah
Praying in the Prophet’s Mosque
Serving wine in Abu Talhah’s house
Busy at work in the date orchard
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 5580 and Sahih Muslim 1980; hearing the announcement Abu Talhah said, pour it out.

quiz.q: Staking money in a phone game and saying ‘it’s just entertainment’ repeats which argument?
o: This is not gambling, this is charity
This is not wine, this is a drink
This is not usury, this is profit
This is not theft, this is a loan
quiz.e: The Jahili Arabs too would give away the meat and say, this is not gambling; this is charity.

quiz.q: What does the lesson say about lending ten thousand in a village and taking twelve at the month’s end?
o: It is merely ordinary business profit
Both are in that list of four
It is part of family help
It is the regular rule for returning a loan
quiz.e: Hadith 1598 of Sahih Muslim; the one who eats it, the one who gives it, the one who writes it, and the one who witnesses it; all are equal.

quiz.q: How did the Qur’an answer the argument ‘in this age one cannot manage without usury’?
o: Permission to take usury at a time of need
An order to reduce the rate of usury
Trade is made lawful, usury is made unlawful
A chance to settle the usury account later
quiz.e: In verse 275 of Surah al-Baqarah the answer is given after setting out their argument ‘trade is just like usury’.

quiz.q: Of the four habits of Jahiliyyah the Prophet ﷺ said would remain even in the Ummah, two are related to
o: Lineage, that is, pride and taunting
Wealth, that is, miserliness and wastefulness
Speech, that is, lying and backbiting
Food, that is, wastefulness and greed
quiz.e: Hadith 934 of Sahih Muslim; the other two are asking for rain through the stars and wailing for the dead.

quiz.q: What the lesson says was missing in the life of Imru’ al-Qays is
o: A purpose
Enough intelligence
The necessary courage
Sufficient wealth
quiz.e: What he had was a revenge; and revenge makes a person run, yes, but takes him nowhere.

quiz.q: What came in hadith 3925 of Sahih al-Bukhari about Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA)?
o: He was the very first to accept Islam in Madinah; this is how it is generally held
He and Ibn Umm Maktum (RA) were the first to come to Madinah
He built the first mosque in Madinah
He was appointed the first judge of Madinah
quiz.e: Al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA) says, they used to teach people the Qur’an.

quiz.q: When giving Zayd ibn Thabit (RA) the responsibility of compiling the Qur’an, what did Abu Bakr (RA) tell him?
o: You are the greatest scholar among us
You are the closest companion of the Prophet ﷺ
Your memory is the sharpest of all
You are a young man, intelligent; we have no suspicion about you
quiz.e: Hadith 4986 of Sahih al-Bukhari; he also said, you used to write the revelation for the Prophet ﷺ.

quiz.q: On hours passing on the phone at night when going to sleep, which action does the lesson point to?
o: Switching the phone completely off
Fixing a set time for night phone use
Sleeping with the phone outside the bed
Making a habit of reading a book before sleep
quiz.e: Along with standing up once on hearing the Fajr adhan; the change begins from there.
